passages.title: The Dragon's Riddle
passages.text: 'I am the one thing that grows smaller the more of me you take, and larger the more of me you leave behind,' the dragon intoned, its voice like pages turning in a vast and ancient book. The apprentice hesitated. To answer wrongly was to forfeit her memories; to refuse was to forfeit the library. She thought of the corridors she had walked that morning, each one stretching further behind her. 'Footsteps,' she whispered. The dragon's eyes narrowed — not, she realised, in anger, but in something perilously close to delight.

questions.q: What is the answer to the riddle?
questions.explain: The more steps you take, the more you leave behind.

questions.q: What was at stake for the apprentice?
questions.explain: Wrong = lose memories; refuse = lose the library.

questions.q: What does the dragon's reaction suggest?

passages.title: The Ferryman
passages.text: Translation is often described as a bridge between languages, yet the metaphor flatters the process. A bridge implies that both banks are fixed and that the traveller arrives unchanged. In truth, every translation alters what it carries: idioms are reshaped, connotations shed or acquired, rhythms broken and rebuilt. The translator is less a bridge-builder than a ferryman who must decide, with each crossing, which cargo can survive the water.

questions.q: Why does the writer reject the 'bridge' metaphor?
options: Bridges are too expensive a metaphor to use.
Translators have always disliked bridge imagery.
It is an old-fashioned image no longer in use.
questions.explain: '…the traveller arrives unchanged' — untrue of translation.

questions.q: What does the ferryman image emphasise?
options: choices about what to keep and what to lose
the speed at which a skilled translator works
the danger of translating across rough water
the high cost of travelling between languages
questions.explain: '…decide… which cargo can survive the water.'

questions.q: What is the tone of the passage?
questions.explain: A careful argument built through metaphor.

passages.title: Unflinchingly Honest?
passages.text: Critics have hailed the novel as 'unflinchingly honest', a phrase that has become so ubiquitous in reviews as to be almost meaningless. What the book offers is not honesty so much as an aesthetic of confession: carefully arranged disclosures that flatter the narrator even as they appear to expose her. That this is done with considerable skill is undeniable; whether it amounts to candour is another matter.

questions.q: What does the writer think of the phrase 'unflinchingly honest'?
questions.explain: 'So ubiquitous… as to be almost meaningless.'

questions.q: How does the writer see the narrator's confessions?
questions.explain: 'Carefully arranged disclosures that flatter the narrator.'

questions.q: What is the writer's overall judgement?
options: a complete failure on every level
a perfect novel without any flaws

passages.title: From Access to Discernment
passages.text: Few institutions have proved as adaptable as the public library. Once guardians of scarce printed matter, they now find themselves curating an abundance of information, much of it of dubious provenance. Their value, accordingly, has shifted from access to discernment: not 'here is what exists' but 'here is what can be trusted'. Whether funding bodies grasp this shift is, regrettably, far from certain.

questions.q: How has the library's value changed?
options: from giving access to helping judge reliability
from lending printed books to running computer games
from offering free services to charging for them
from serving the public to serving private clients
very old and in poor physical condition
written by famous and respected authors
Funders may not understand the new role.
Libraries are closing faster than ever before.
People simply don't read printed books any more.
Librarians are not trained to judge information.
questions.explain: 'Whether funding bodies grasp this shift is… far from certain.'

passages.title: The Weather of Her Sentences
passages.text: She said she would think about it, which, in our family, was the politest form of no. We had all learnt to read the weather of her sentences: the long pause that meant disappointment, the brisk 'Lovely' that closed a subject for good. So when she said, after a silence that seemed to empty the room, 'Well, your grandfather would have liked that,' we did not know whether to celebrate or to grieve.

questions.q: What did 'I'll think about it' mean in this family?
What does 'the weather of her sentences' refer to?
options: the hidden emotional signals in how she spoke
her habit of always talking about the weather first
how loudly or softly she usually spoke at dinner
the travel plans she made for the family each year
questions.explain: Pauses and tone revealed her feelings.

questions.q: Why didn't they know how to react?
options: Her remark could signal approval or sorrow.
She spoke too quietly for anyone to hear her.
They had never met or known their grandfather.
She was obviously joking, but nobody laughed.
questions.explain: It invokes the late grandfather — approval mixed with grief.
